translations: Today is Saturday. My friend and I are going to watch football. We take a taxi there.
There are lots of people. Everyone is very happy. I like the team in red. Their numbers look great.
The match is great. Our team won! My friend says, "Let's come again next week." I say, "OK!"
My older brother loves playing football. He plays every Wednesday and Saturday. His team is small, only twelve people.
This afternoon my brother has a match. Mum, Dad and I all go to watch. The weather is nice, not cold and not hot. We sit at the front.
The match starts. The other team is tall, and fast too. The first goal is theirs. Mum says, "It doesn't matter, there's still time."
In the second half my brother plays really well. He runs fast and scores a goal! We all stand up and shout, "Go, brother!"
In the end it's one-all. My brother is a bit tired, but happy. In the evening we go to a restaurant together. My brother eats lots of rice.
Dad asks me, "Do you want to play football too?" I think about it and say, "I do! Tomorrow I'll go and learn with my brother."

translations: I like buying old clothes. Today I saw a black jacket online.
This jacket is very big, and very nice-looking. It's Japanese, over twenty years old.
I ask the seller, "How much?" The seller says, "Three hundred kuai." I say, "Too expensive! Two hundred, is that OK?" The seller says, "Fine." I'm so happy!
Xiao Lin is my friend. She has a small shop behind the school. The clothes in the shop are all old, but they all look great.
On Sunday morning I go to her shop. There aren't many people. Xiao Lin is drinking tea. She says, "You're here! Sit down."
I see a white piece of clothing. It's very long and very big. Xiao Lin says, "This one is from the nineties, made by a Japanese designer."
I ask, "How much?" Xiao Lin says, "Five hundred kuai." I say, "A bit expensive." She laughs: "You're my friend, four hundred then."
I put it on. The me in the mirror looks so different! Xiao Lin says, "It looks great, buy it."
I buy it. On the way home I'm very happy. Mum sees it and asks, "Are these new clothes?" I say, "No, they're old, but I love them."
I really like watching Japanese anime. Every evening I watch for an hour.
Today's anime is really good. A little cat wants to find its home. It walks for many days and is very tired.
In the end it finds its home. Its mother is waiting for it at the door. I cried. My little sister says, "Brother, why are you crying?"

stories.title_en: I want to go to Japan
translations: I'm a student, nineteen this year. I love Japanese anime. There are lots of anime books in my room.
My favourite anime is a boy's story. He has no home and no money. But he has lots of friends.
He and his friends go somewhere very far away. Lots happens on the way, some good, some bad. They aren't afraid.
My friend David likes this anime too. We watch it together every Friday. We eat, drink tea, watch anime and chat.
David asks me, "Do you want to go to Japan?" I say, "Yes! I want to go to Tokyo and see the places in the anime."
Now I study a little Japanese every day. Next year I want to go to Japan with David. We'll fly there!

translations: Tomorrow I'm going to Beijing. I'm flying there; the plane leaves at ten in the morning.
Beijing is very big and has lots of people. I want to look around the schools and shops. I also want to eat Beijing food.
My Chinese friend works in Beijing. He says, "I'll come and find you at the airport." I'm so happy. See you tomorrow!

translations: I arrived in Shanghai yesterday. Shanghai is very big and very beautiful. The weather is a bit hot, so I wore a white top.
In the morning I went to a restaurant. The waiter asked me, "What would you like to eat?" I said, "I'd like noodles and a cup of tea." The noodles were delicious and not expensive.
After eating I wanted to go to the shops. I didn't know the way, so I asked an old man, "Excuse me, where is the shop?" He said, "Up ahead, five minutes' walk."
The shop had lots of things. I bought a cup and some fruit. The woman selling things was very nice. She said, "Your Chinese is very good!" I smiled.
In the afternoon I took a taxi back to the hotel. The driver asked me, "Where are you from?" I said, "I'm British." He said, "Welcome to Shanghai!"
In the evening I called my mum. I said, "Shanghai is great, I really like it here." Tomorrow I want to go and see Shanghai's river.
I get up at seven every day. First I drink a glass of water, then eat a little rice.
At eight I take the bus to school. There are lots of people on the bus, and I don't get a seat.
Class starts at nine. The teacher says, "Hello, everyone!" We say, "Hello, teacher!" Today we're studying characters. I love writing Chinese characters.

translations: Today is Sunday, and it's raining outside. I don't want to go out, so I stay at home.
In the morning I read in bed. The story in the book is very interesting. I read for two hours and got a bit tired.
At noon I want to cook. At home there's rice, eggs and some vegetables. I make egg fried rice. It doesn't look great, but it's delicious!
In the afternoon my friend Xiao Wang calls me. She asks, "What are you doing?" I say, "I'm at home, it's raining outside." She says, "I'll come to yours, let's watch a film together."
At three Xiao Wang arrives. She's bought lots of fruit. We sit together and watch a Chinese film. The film is great and we both laugh.
In the evening the rain stops. Xiao Wang goes home. I think: a rainy Sunday is nice too.
I'm a university student. I have two thousand kuai a month.
Food costs eight hundred, taxis cost two hundred. I also like buying clothes and books.
This month I bought too many things. I only have a hundred left! I think: next month I'll buy a bit less and learn more about how to use money.
My dad has a small shop. It's in front of our house and sells fruit, tea and a few small things.
Every morning at six Dad goes to the shop. He's very busy, but he really likes this job.
On Saturday I don't have class, so I go to the shop to see Dad. Dad says, "Good timing! Lots of people today, give me a hand."
A woman wants to buy apples. She asks, "How much are the apples per jin?" I say, "Eight kuai a jin." She buys three jin. I say, "Twenty-four kuai." She gives me thirty and I give her six.
In the afternoon Dad asks, "How much did we sell today?" I check and say, "One thousand two hundred kuai!" Dad is very happy.
In the evening Dad says, "Doing business isn't easy. Study hard at university, and later you can be my boss!" We both laugh.

translations: David and I wanted to go to the weekend football match. But when we opened our phones, the tickets had already sold out.
David said, "Never mind, let's watch it at a bar." The bar was packed, and everyone was wearing red.
The match was brilliant. In the end our team won two-one. Everyone sang together; it was even more fun than being at the stadium!

translations: Our university football team got a new goalkeeper called Xiao Ma. He's very tall, but doesn't say much.
At his first training session Xiao Ma was a bit nervous. He didn't catch a single ball kicked at him. Some people laughed at him, and his face went red.
After training I went over and said, "Don't worry, everyone's like this on day one." Xiao Ma said, "Thanks. I used to play in a small city; people here play so fast."
From that day on, Xiao Ma went to the pitch at six every morning to practise. Rain or cold, he went. Sometimes I trained with him.
A month later we had a very important match. The other team shot many times, but Xiao Ma stopped them all. In the end we won one-nil.
After the match everyone lifted Xiao Ma up. He smiled and said, "My friend helped me." Hearing that made me really happy.

translations: My grandpa is seventy-five this year. When he was young he loved football and went to the stadium every weekend. Now his legs aren't good, so he can only watch on TV at home.
One day I was looking for something in Grandpa's room and found a very old box. Inside was a red and white football shirt. It had gone a bit yellow, and it had a "9" on the back.
I took the shirt to Grandpa and asked, "Whose is this?" When he saw it, his eyes lit up. He said, "It's mine! Fifty years ago I played for the factory team. I was number nine."
Grandpa told me their team wasn't big and had no money. They bought their own boots, and the pitch was a tiny patch of ground. But everyone was serious and trained every day after work.
"In our best year we beat every factory team in the city," Grandpa said, laughing. "That night we all went out to eat, drank a lot and sang all night."

I asked Grandpa, "Would you like to watch a match at the stadium again?" He said, "I'd like to, but I can't walk that far." I thought for a moment and said, "I'll take you! We'll drive, and I'll push your wheelchair."
The next Saturday Grandpa and I went to the stadium. He wore his old shirt, and lots of people looked at him. A young man came over and said, "Grandpa, your shirt is so cool!"
During the match Grandpa kept shouting and laughing, as if he'd become young again. On the way home he held my hand and said, "Thank you, child. Today was the happiest day I've had in years."

I took out a long black skirt. Its shape was simple, but it was beautifully made. I asked Mum, "Where did you buy this?"
Mum smiled and said, "I bought it in Tokyo when I was twenty. It cost me a month's wages back then." I was amazed.
I looked it up on my phone and found it was made by a famous Japanese designer. Now this skirt goes for over five thousand kuai online!
Mum said, "If you like it, take it. I can't wear it any more anyway." I said, "No, I won't sell it. I'm going to wear it properly."
Now that skirt is my favourite piece of clothing. Every time I wear it, I think of what Mum was like when she was young.

Lots of people were dressed as anime characters. One boy was dressed exactly like my favourite character, and we even took a photo with him.
Inside there were lots of little stalls selling books, clothes and knick-knacks. My sister bought two manga, and I bought a top with a cat printed on it.
At two in the afternoon an artist arrived. It was the creator of my favourite anime! Everyone wanted his autograph. We queued for an hour.
Finally it was my turn. I was nervous and said in not-very-good Japanese, "I really love your work." He smiled and drew a little cat in my book.
On the way home I kept looking at that little cat. My sister said, "Brother, you're happier today than at New Year."

Half an hour after getting on, I heard the announcement: "Next stop, Nanjing." I got a fright. I'd got on the wrong train!
I asked the attendant straight away. She said, "Don't worry, get off at Nanjing and buy another ticket." In the end I was three hours late, but I got to see Nanjing too.

translations: It's my first time in Chengdu. My friend told me you have to eat hotpot here. So in the evening we went to a famous hotpot restaurant.
The place was hot and noisy, with a red pot on every table. The waiter asked us, "Spicy or not spicy?" I said, "Half and half."
We ordered beef, fish, tofu and lots of vegetables. My friend said, "Meat first, then veg." I copied him and put the beef into the pot.
I took a bite of the spicy side and started coughing straight away, my eyes watering. My friend couldn't stop laughing: "Slowly! Drink some soy milk!"
After a while I got used to it. It's spicy, sure, but it smells and tastes amazing. We ate for over two hours and spent three hundred kuai in total.
On the way back to the hotel I said to my friend, "Let's come again tomorrow night!" He said, "Not scared of spice any more?" I said, "I am, but I like it more!"

translations: Before coming to Beijing I'd already decided: I had to go to the Great Wall. I'd looked at lots of photos online, blue sky, long walls, really beautiful.
That morning I got up at six. The sky was a bit overcast, but I thought it probably wouldn't rain. I took a two-hour bus ride to the foot of the Great Wall.
I started climbing. The Great Wall was much harder to climb than I'd imagined; some parts were very high, some very narrow. After half an hour I was exhausted.
Just then it started to rain. At first it was light, then it got heavier and heavier. I hadn't brought an umbrella, and my clothes were soon soaked. I stood in a little watchtower, feeling fed up.
There was an old man in the watchtower too. He saw me and said with a smile, "Young man, first time here?" I said, "Yes, but the weather is awful."
The old man said, "I've sold water here for twenty years. The Wall is beautiful on sunny days, and beautiful on rainy days too; it's just that few people see it." He gave me a cup of hot tea.

I drank the tea and looked outside. In the rain the Great Wall ran on over the mountains with no end in sight. The mountains were covered in white mist, like a Chinese painting. I took out my phone and took lots of photos.
Half an hour later the rain stopped. I said goodbye to the old man and kept climbing. I didn't see a blue sky that day, but I saw a Great Wall few people get to see.
Now my favourite photo on my phone is the Great Wall in the rain that day. Every time I see it, I remember that cup of hot tea and what the old man said.

translations: This morning, as I was about to leave, I found my phone was missing. I looked on the desk, on the bed, in my bag: it was nowhere.
Without my phone I didn't know the time and couldn't take the metro, because my metro card is on my phone. I was frantic.
Then I remembered I'd gone to the café downstairs last night. Had I left it there? I ran downstairs straight away.
The waitress saw me and said with a smile, "You're here for your phone, right?" She took my phone out from under the counter. I was so happy I nearly jumped.
To say thank you I bought two coffees, one for me and one for her. She said, "No need to thank me. Just don't forget it again."
On the way to work I thought: that half hour without my phone felt longer than a day. Maybe I should use my phone a bit less.

translations: I've just come to China to study, and I need to open a bank account. On Monday morning I took my passport to the bank next to the university.
There were quite a few people in the bank. I took a number first, then sat down to wait. After forty minutes it was finally my turn.
The clerk asked me, "What would you like to do?" I said, "I'd like to open an account." She had me fill in a form with my name, phone number and address.
There was one question I didn't understand, so I asked her. She patiently explained, "Put your job here. You're a student, so write 'student'."
Once it was done she gave me a bank card and showed me how to use it on my phone. I tried it; it's very convenient.
Walking out of the bank, I felt really happy. Now I can pay with my phone, just like Chinese people!

The whole stadium went silent for a second, then everyone went wild. The man next to me hugged me, shouting and jumping. So the best bit of football really is the last minute.

translations: Every Sunday I play in an amateur league on the east side of the city with colleagues. Our team is called "Not Working Monday". The name is funny, but we're not very good.
We hadn't won a single match this season. After every match the captain, Lao Zhang, would say, "Never mind, we'll definitely win next time." Everyone laughed at how optimistic he was.
Last week Lao Zhang made a decision: every Wednesday after work, we'd all train together for an hour. At first only three or four people came, but more and more joined.
We practised passing and movement, and started studying videos of our opponents. Gradually we played better and better together.
Yesterday we played the team top of the league. We scored in the first half. In the second half they attacked non-stop, but we held on.
As soon as the final whistle blew, everyone ran to Lao Zhang. He was too emotional to speak and just kept smiling. That night we celebrated at a barbecue place until late.

translations: My friend Xiao Li has recently got hooked on second-hand designer clothes. He browses online every evening and wants to buy anything he likes.
One day he excitedly sent me a link: "Look, a Comme des Garçons jacket for only a thousand! It was over eight thousand new."
I looked at the photos and something seemed off. The label was too new, and the stitching wasn't very neat. I told him not to rush to pay.
We looked up lots of information together and compared real and fake labels. Sure enough, the font on this jacket's label was different from the real one, and the buttons were wrong too.
Xiao Li was a bit disappointed, but also relieved: "Good thing you warned me, otherwise that thousand would've been wasted."
Since then Xiao Li always checks carefully before buying. He says, "When buying second-hand clothes, your eyes matter more than your wallet."

translations: Near our university there's a very old street, and at the end of it is a tiny tailor's shop. There's no sign outside, just an old pair of scissors hanging by the door.

The first time I went in was because I'd bought a very long pair of trousers at a second-hand market and wanted them shortened. The shop was dark, with fabric everywhere, and an old master with completely white hair was sewing.

The old tailor's surname was Chen, and he'd been a tailor for fifty years. He looked at my trousers, felt the fabric and said, "These aren't ordinary trousers. They're made in Japan, and the fabric is excellent. It'd be a shame to cut them."
I was surprised and asked how he knew. Master Chen smiled: "Fifty years in, you can tell by touch. Look at the thread here: every stitch is neat. Few people make things like this now."
Instead of cutting the trousers, he sewed a small hem on the inside. "This way, if you want them long later, just unpick the thread." I tried them on; the length was perfect.

After that I often went to Master Chen's shop. Sometimes to alter clothes, sometimes just to drink tea and hear his old stories. He said that in the eighties everyone had their clothes made, and there was a long queue outside his shop every day.
"Now everyone buys cheap clothes at the mall and throws them away after a year," Master Chen said a little sadly. "Clothes are like people: you have to spend time with them before you get attached."

Last month I heard the street was going to be demolished. I went to find Master Chen straight away. He was packing up and seemed calm. He gave me a small pair of scissors and said, "From now on, learn to alter your own clothes."
Now those scissors sit on my desk. Every time I buy an old piece of clothing, I look carefully at its thread and fabric first, as if Master Chen were still beside me.

translations: I've loved drawing since I was little. In secondary school I decided to draw my own manga, about a talking robot and a little girl.
I drew for two hours every day after school. Drawing people was hard, especially hands and eyes. I drew them again and again until my desk was covered in paper.
Three months later I finally finished chapter one, twenty pages in total. I put it online, nervous that no one would read it.
On the first day only ten people read it, on the second a hundred, and a week later five thousand people had read it. Lots of people commented: "Hurry up with the next chapter!"
One reader wrote me a very long letter. She said that while she was ill in hospital she read my manga every day, and the little robot made her feel less lonely.
When I finished the letter I cried. For the first time I understood that what I draw can help other people. I told myself: however tired I get, I'll finish this story.

translations: From Beijing to Kunming, I chose a train of over thirty hours. My friends all thought I was mad: flying only takes four.
I'd bought a sleeper berth. In the same compartment were an elderly couple and a young soldier. At first nobody talked; everyone just looked at their phones.
In the evening the old lady took out a big bag of mandarins and insisted on sharing them. That's how everyone gradually started chatting.

The couple were going to Kunming to see their grandson; they hadn't seen him for three years. The soldier had just gone on leave and was heading back to his home town in Yunnan. He said his mum would definitely have a whole table of food waiting.
In the middle of the night I couldn't sleep, so I stood by the window. Outside was pitch black, with just a few lights at the odd small station we passed. The train's rhythm was soothing.
The next afternoon the train reached Kunming. As we got off, the old lady held my hand and said, "Take care on your way, child." In that moment the thirty hours didn't feel long at all.

translations: This September I started sharing a flat with two people: Xiao Zhou, who does design, and A-Ming, who works at a hospital.
At first there were lots of problems between us. Xiao Zhou likes drawing at night and often doesn't sleep until two or three. A-Ming has to get up at five for work, so he never slept well.
The kitchen was another problem. Everyone thought everyone else didn't wash up. One day A-Ming stuck a note on the fridge: "Please clean the kitchen after using it."
That evening we finally sat down and had a proper talk. Everyone said what they thought and listened to the others' difficulties.
In the end we agreed a few rules: quiet after midnight; take turns cleaning the kitchen; eat a meal together at weekends.
Two months on, we get along better and better. On Sunday evenings the three of us cook and chat together; it feels like a family.

So I started tracking my spending on my phone, recording every payment. A week later I got a shock: I'd spent over two hundred on bubble tea alone!
Now I look over my spending every week. Keeping accounts hasn't made me richer, but it's made me clearer about what I really need.

translations: In my third year I applied for an internship at an accounting firm. The day I got the interview invitation I was too excited to sleep.
The week before the interview I prepared every day. I revised my course material and got a friend to play the interviewer so I could practise answering questions.
On the day I wore my new suit and arrived half an hour early. While I waited my hands wouldn't stop sweating.
The interviewer's first question was simple: "Why did you choose accounting?" I said I like numbers, because numbers don't lie. She smiled.
The questions got harder and harder. There was one about tax I just couldn't answer. I had to be honest: "Sorry, I'm not clear on that yet, but I'll go back and study it properly."
A week later I got an email: I'd passed! The manager later told me they liked my honesty. So telling the truth when you don't know is a skill too.

translations: Last year my cousin opened a bubble tea shop in the university district. When it opened business was great, with a long queue every day. But six months later she called me, sounding exhausted.
"You study accounting, can you look at my books?" she said. "The shop's busy every day, but at the end of the month there's never enough money."
At the weekend I went to her shop. Her books were a mess: some in a notebook, some on her phone, and some not recorded at all. It took me two full days to sort out six months of accounts.

The problems soon became clear. One: rent was too high, a third of revenue. Two: she prepared lots of fresh fruit every day, but it didn't sell by evening and had to be thrown away. Three: the delivery platform took a twenty percent fee.
My cousin looked at the spreadsheet I'd made and said nothing for ages. Finally she said, "So I've been busy all this time, but not making money."

We came up with a few ideas together. Instead of preparing a whole day's fruit at once, she'd prep it three times a day. She cut a few slow-selling drinks from the menu. She also started selling homemade cakes, because cakes have a higher margin than bubble tea.

Most importantly, I made her a simple spreadsheet so she could spend ten minutes on the books after closing each day. At first she found it a hassle, but then she found that seeing the numbers every day gave her real peace of mind.
Three months later my cousin called again. This time she sounded happy: "We finally made a profit this month!" She said she'd treat me to a year of bubble tea.
I laughed: "Then I'm going to get fat." After hanging up I felt, for the first time, that the accounting in my textbooks really could help someone make their dream come true.

translations: Lots of people think a football club only has players and coaches, but many people work behind the scenes. My cousin is a data analyst at a professional club.
His job is to compile the data from every match: how many kilometres each player ran, their pass completion rate, where they lose the ball most. In the end all these numbers go to the head coach.
My cousin says data can sometimes reveal problems the eye can't see. For example, last year the team kept conceding in the last fifteen minutes. Everyone assumed the players lacked stamina.
But after studying the data, my cousin found the problem wasn't stamina but the timing of substitutions. The coach always subbed too late; the new players hadn't got into the game before it was over.
The coach took his advice and made substitutions ten minutes earlier. In the final stretch of that season the team conceded half as many goals.
I asked my cousin whether data would make football boring. He smiled: "Data can only tell you what happened. The most brilliant strike in a match will always come from a person."

translations: My little sister Xiaoyu started playing football at eight. Back then her school only had a boys' team, and every day after school she'd stand on the sidelines and watch, often for an hour.

One day the coach came over and asked, "Do you want to play too?" Xiaoyu nodded. The coach thought about it and let her train with the boys. At first many of the boys didn't want to pass to her, thinking girls couldn't play.

Xiaoyu didn't complain; she just trained harder than everyone else. If others trained for an hour, she trained for two. After a term she was the fastest player on the team, and the boys started passing to her of their own accord.

In middle school Xiaoyu joined the city girls' team. Training was really tough: she had to get up at half five every morning to run. At weekends, while her classmates went out, she practised shooting on the pitch over and over.
At first our family didn't all agree. Grandma thought football was too dangerous for a girl, and that she'd never find a good job. Mum and Dad supported her but worried about her studies.

To prove herself, Xiaoyu set herself a rule: however tired she was from training, she'd always finish her homework. She often memorised vocabulary on the bus home and did homework until eleven at night. That year her grades actually got better.

Last summer Xiaoyu's team entered the national championship. On the day of the final our whole family went to watch, even Grandma. In the last few minutes it was still nil-nil, when Xiaoyu suddenly shot from outside the box and the ball flew straight into the top right corner.
The whole stand rose to its feet. I turned and saw Grandma clapping and wiping away tears. She said loudly to the person next to her, "That's my granddaughter!"
Now Xiaoyu has had offers from several universities. She says she wants to be a coach one day, so more girls who want to play won't have to stand on the sidelines and watch.

Only later did I realise this is called "deconstruction". The designer deliberately takes clothes apart so you can see the structure normally hidden inside, and rethink how a garment is made.
Now I pay attention to details when I dress too. A good piece of clothing isn't just nice outside; it's just as carefully made inside.

translations: My friend A-Jie is a collector who specialises in work by Japanese designers from the nineties. His flat has a room just for clothes, with temperature and humidity strictly controlled.
His clothes aren't for wearing. Each one is numbered, with the runway photos and magazine coverage from the time kept alongside. He says it isn't a wardrobe; it's an archive.
Once he showed me a black jacket. From the outside it looked ordinary, but turned inside out, it was covered in handwritten poems. It was a sample the designer made only three of for one show.
A-Jie spent five whole years looking for that jacket. He finally found it in an old man's storeroom in Osaka. The old man didn't know what it was worth and charged him very little.
I asked whether he felt bad about that. A-Jie was silent for a moment, then said he'd gone back, paid the old man more, and taken him out for a meal.
He said, "Collecting isn't just owning, it's protecting. One day these clothes will be in a museum, so more people can see the ideas of that era."

The teacher had me voice a character who was crying. I read it over a dozen times, and every time the teacher said "no emotion". It turns out emotion in the voice is even harder to express than on the face.
Since then, when I watch anime I always pay special attention to the voice actors' performances. Every line might have been practised dozens of times.

translations: There's one anime film I've watched at least ten times. The story takes place near a small station in Tokyo, and the visuals are incredibly realistic; even the vending machines by the road are drawn in detail.
Last year when I travelled to Japan, I spent a whole day finding places from the film. Online this kind of trip is called a "pilgrimage".
Following an online guide, I found the station first. Standing on the platform, it looked exactly like the film; I was so excited I nearly shouted.

Next was the long staircase. In the film, the two leads meet here for the last time. There were already several young people on the stairs taking photos, holding up screenshots on their phones to find the angle.
We didn't know each other, but we started chatting naturally. A girl from Taiwan told me it was her third visit, and each time she noticed new details.

That evening I sat alone on the stairs watching the sunset. I suddenly realised that what I love isn't just the film, but what it makes me believe: however far apart two people go, one day they'll meet again.

translations: After graduating I joined a small animation studio. At the interview I showed them my portfolio. The boss looked at it for a long time and said just one thing: "Start tomorrow."
On my first day I discovered that reality was nothing like I'd imagined. I thought I'd be designing characters straight away; instead I was assigned to draw in-betweens.

In-betweens are all the frames that fill the gap between two key poses drawn by a key animator. If someone turns their head, the key animator draws only the start and end; the dozen or so frames in between are drawn by newcomers like me.
The work was incredibly tedious and exhausting. I drew over a hundred frames a day, earning less than ten kuai per frame. Finishing at midnight was normal, and I often worked weekends.
For a while I really wanted to quit. I began to wonder whether I actually liked making animation, or just liked watching it.

Right then, a veteran key animator at the studio noticed me. His name was Mr Lin, and he'd been in the industry thirty years. He went through my drawings one by one and pointed out many problems I'd never considered.
"Your drawing is clean, but it has no weight," he said. "When someone jumps down, their clothes, hair and body all land at different moments. Observe life first, then animate."
From that day, every time I took the metro I watched people: how they walked, how they turned, how their bags swung. My notebook filled with sketches. Slowly my in-betweens came to life.

Two years later I was allowed to draw key animation for the first time. It was a shot of a little girl running in the rain, only three seconds long. On the night it aired, I stared at the screen, watching it again and again.
The end credits were long, and my name was near the end, so small it was almost unreadable. But to me those were the best three seconds in the world.

After coming back I realised that sometimes the point of travelling isn't where you go, but who you become along the way.

translations: On my last day in Guangzhou, as I got ready for the airport, I suddenly found my passport was gone. I went through my suitcase three times and still couldn't find it. Take-off was only five hours away.
My first reaction was panic; my mind went blank. The woman at the hotel reception saw the state I was in, sat me down with a glass of water, then helped me think it through step by step.

First she called the restaurant I'd been to the day before, but it wasn't there. Then she suggested I go straight to the local police station to report it, because replacing a passport requires a police report.
At the police station an officer patiently helped me fill in the form and gave me the consulate's address and phone number. I had to change my flight and stay in Guangzhou three more days.
On the third day the police station called: a taxi driver had found my passport in his car and handed it in. It had slipped out of my jacket pocket.
I wanted to thank the driver in person, but he hadn't left his name. I wrote a long post online thanking all the strangers in the city who'd helped me.

In the evening the internet came back, but I didn't open my phone straight away. That day made me realise that often it's us who don't want to leave the internet.

translations: Below my flat there's a noodle shop that's been open for over twenty years. It's tiny, only six tables, but it's packed every lunchtime.
The owner's surname is He, and everyone calls him Uncle He. He gets up at four every morning to knead dough and simmer the broth. He says the broth needs six hours to taste right.

In my four years at university I went almost every week. Uncle He remembered I don't eat coriander and reminded the kitchen every time. When he saw I was stressed about exams, he'd sneak me an extra egg.
After graduating I moved to another city for work. The first time I came home, I dropped my bags and went straight to the noodle shop. The first thing Uncle He said was: "Still no coriander?"
In that moment my eyes welled up. In the year away I'd eaten at lots of fancy restaurants, but no bowl of noodles had made me feel like that.

Uncle He says he plans to work five more years and then retire. I asked what would happen to the shop. He smiled: "My son's learning. The craft can't die out; people on this street still need their noodles."

translations: At university my finance lecturer wrote a question on the board: "If you improve by one percent every day, what happens after a year?"

We worked it out: the answer is over thirty-seven times where you started. The lecturer said that's the power of compounding: at first you can't see a difference, but over time the gap grows and grows.
Since then I've put a small amount into investments every month. It's not much, but I trust time to do the rest.

translations: January to March every year is the busiest time at an accounting firm; everyone calls it "busy season". In my first year interning at a firm, I finally understood what that meant.
Our team was auditing a furniture company. In the first week my job was reconciling their bank statements with their ledger; every payment in and out had to match.
One night at ten I found a payment of five hundred thousand with no contract. I was nervous; I didn't know whether I'd misread something or there was really a problem.

I told the manager what I'd found. Rather than criticise me for wasting time, she praised me for being careful. The next day she came with me to ask the company's finance staff, and we learned it was an equipment payment whose contract hadn't been filed yet.
Although it turned out to be fine, the manager said that's the whole point of auditing: never let a single question go.
At the end of March the audit report was finally submitted. That evening the whole team went for hotpot. I was so tired I could barely keep my eyes open, but I felt a real sense of achievement.
